lessons.title: डोळा (ḍoḷā) — the letter you've heard since Chapter 5, formally
lessons.gloss: eye — carrying Marathi's signature extra letter ळ, and a word that started life meaning something else entirely

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: मित्र, कुटुंब, भाऊ, बहीण (mitra, kuṭumb, bhāū, bahīṇ) — the people you'd introduce. This chapter turns to the body you'd ask after when you check how someone is.
डोळा — ḍoḷā — eye (masculine).

ड you have from āvaḍṇe; ो the familiar o mark, from bolṇe. Then ळ — the retroflex "l" you first met, unlabeled, inside Chapter 5's काळजी. Formally: tongue curled back, same place as ट and ण. Standard Hindi dropped this sound centuries ago; Marathi kept it, sharing it with the Dravidian languages to the south and with Gujarati. Ḍo-ḷā.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — not the old eye-word at all

segments.text: डोळा (ḍoḷā) continues Maharastri Prakrit ḍola, "eye," from Sanskrit दोल dola — "a swing, a swinging." Somewhere in Prakrit, "a swinging thing" came to mean "eye," and that word pushed out the one you might expect: the true inherited Indo-Aryan eye-word is Sanskrit अक्षि/अक्ष akṣi/akṣa, from Indo-European h₃ekʷ-, the very cousin of Latin oculus and English eye. Hindi's आँख ā̃kh continues that old word, worn down through Prakrit acchi. Marathi's eye is not that word at all — it is a replacement, built on something that once just meant swing.

lessons.title: कान (kān) — an ear, and a cluster you've seen simplify before
lessons.gloss: ear — a consonant cluster simplified the same way don copied teen, and a root disputed among Sanskrit scholars

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called The letters in this word and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: डोळा (ḍoḷā) — its own root turned out to be a surprise, a swing, not the old eye-word. This next word has a different kind of surprise: not what it meant, but how its middle got simpler.
कान — kān — ear (masculine).
Nothing new. क, ा, न are all familiar from Chapter 1 onward. Kā-n.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: a cluster ground down, like Chapter 7's दोन

segments.text: कान continues Sanskrit कर्ण karṇa. Getting there took the same kind of step Chapter 7 traced in दोन: Prakrit could not keep Sanskrit's consonant cluster rṇ intact, so it simplified — not by copying a neighbor this time, but by doubling the surviving consonant, rṇ becomes ṇṇ, giving Prakrit कण्ण kaṇṇa. Old Marathi then simplified the geminate back down to one ṇ with a lengthened vowel: kāna. Different cluster, different path, same underlying habit — Prakrit does not tolerate what Sanskrit could pack into one syllable.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a disputed root

segments.text: Past Sanskrit, कर्ण's own origin is genuinely disputed among scholars — proposals connect it to a word for "point, spike," to a root for "handle, grip," even to the verb "to hear," but none has won general acceptance. Rather than choose one and present it as settled, this lesson names the dispute and stops there, the same honest gap Chapter 12 named for कुटुंब, and the same restraint that kept बहीण from being handed a false cousin — बहीण looks like it should match English sister, and does not.

segments.instruction: karṇa becomes kaṇṇa becomes kāna, the cluster ground down and then simplified again
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: *karṇa* → *kaṇṇa* → *kāna*, the cluster ground down and then simplified again]

segments.text: What did Prakrit do to Sanskrit कर्ण's rṇ cluster? (Doubled it to ṇṇ, then Old Marathi simplified that back to one ṇ.) Is कर्ण's root beyond Sanskrit settled? (No — disputed.) Which Chapter 7 word also showed a consonant cluster changing shape? (दोन, whose final n came from copying तीन.)
Sources: Wiktionary: कान (kān).

lessons.title: तोंड (tõḍ) — the mouth, and the formal word standing behind it
lessons.gloss: mouth — the everyday word, beside a formal Sanskrit doublet you already half-know

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: डोळा (ḍoḷā), कान (kān) — eye, ear. Recall how कान (kān)'s middle got simpler — rṇ doubled to ṇṇ, then simplified again. One more word before the chapter's closing one.
तोंड — tõḍ — mouth (neuter).
Nothing new. त, ो, ं, ड are all familiar. Tõ-ḍ, the anusvāra nasalizing the o.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the everyday word, and its formal twin

segments.text: तोंड (tõḍ) continues Maharastri Prakrit तुंड tuṃḍa, from Sanskrit तुण्ड tuṇḍa, "mouth, snout, beak" — a tadbhava, worn down the way भाऊ was. Marathi keeps a second, formal word for the same thing: मुख mukh, borrowed whole from Sanskrit exactly the way मित्र and कुटुंब were — the same everyday-versus-formal split कुटुंब's chapter didn't need to show you for a body part until now. You'll hear तोंड (tõḍ) in daily speech and मुख in writing, formal address, and words like mukhya, "chief, principal" — literally "at the mouth/face of things."

segments.instruction: three so far — ḍoḷā, kān, tõḍ
segments.source: [YOU SAY: three so far — **ḍoḷā, kān, tõḍ**]

segments.text: What is तोंड (tõḍ)'s formal Sanskrit doublet? (मुख, mukh.) Is तोंड (tõḍ) itself borrowed whole or worn down? (Worn down — a tadbhava, like भाऊ.)
Sources: Wiktionary: तोंड (tõḍ).

lessons.title: नाक (nāk) — the face, completed
lessons.gloss: nose — completing the face, and the one of the four with the most secure English cousin

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: डोळा, कान, तोंड (ḍoḷā, kān, tõḍ) — say them. One face part left, and it is the one with the plainest history of the four.
नाक — nāk — nose (neuter).
Nothing new. न, ा, क — all familiar since Chapter 1. Nā-k.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the secure cousin of "nose"

segments.text: नाक (nāk) continues Prakrit णक्क ṇakka, "nose," built on Sanskrit नस् nas-, "nose," plus a suffix. You may have met the other Sanskrit route to "nose," नासिका nāsikā, elsewhere — Marathi's नाक (nāk) took the shorter one, straight from the bare root. Either way the destination is the same Indo-European neh₂s-, which English inherited directly as nose. Of this chapter's four words, नाक (nāk) is the one whose English cousin needs no qualification at all.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — four words, four kinds of history

segments.text: Run the face back one more time, and notice each word told a different kind of story: डोळा (ḍoḷā) replaced its old Indo-Aryan word entirely, with something that once just meant swing; कान (kān)'s root is honestly disputed, even though its rṇ becomes ṇṇ becomes ṇ path is not; तोंड (tõḍ) keeps a formal Sanskrit doublet, मुख, standing beside it; and नाक (nāk) is the plainest of the four — a straight, secure line to Sanskrit and to English both. Not every word in a family carries the same amount of history, and knowing which is which is worth more than assuming they all match.
